The library ships several model generations under one roof, and the registry treats them uniformly. Demucs itself (Demucs, L219) is the original: a purely waveform-domain U-Net with a BLSTM bottleneck, encoder blocks built from convolution, a DConv residual branch (DConv, L86), and skip connections back up the decoder. HDemucs (HDemucs, L338) added the spectrogram branch. HTDemucs (HTDemucs, L27) is the v4 model that adds the transformer and remains the default — DEFAULT_MODEL, L24 is literally the string htdemucs, and the loader prints a notice reminding you the default changed from the older MDX checkpoints.

All sources are predicted jointly: the standard four are drums, bass, other, and vocals. A forward pass returns a tensor of shape [batch, sources, channels, samples], and the loss during training is computed in the time domain, backpropagating through the masking and inverse STFT. That design choice — end-to-end differentiable decoding rather than a separate spectral loss — is what makes the hybrid branches cleanly combinable.

The Hybrid Front End: Waveform and Spectrogram

HTDemucs.forward starts by padding the mixture to the training segment length — ten seconds at 44.1 kHz by default — because convolution alignment is easier when every call sees the same geometry. Then _spec (HTDemucs._spec, L420) pads the signal by three quarters of the kernel, calls spectro, L11 (a thin wrapper over torch.stft with a Hann window), and trims the edges so the STFT output lines up sample-for-sample with the waveform branch. The FFT size is 4096 with a hop of 1024.

A detail that matters: the released model uses complex as channels (cac=True), so instead of predicting a magnitude mask and running EM refinement, _magnitude (HTDemucs._magnitude, L452) reshapes the complex spectrogram into real channels, the network predicts full complex spectra for each source, and _mask (HTDemucs._mask, L463) simply reinterprets them — the OpenUnmix Wiener path in _wiener (HTDemucs._wiener, L480) stays available for the older non-CaC configurations. The two branches then run through matched stacks of HEncLayer (HEncLayer, L69) and HDecLayer (HDecLayer, L256) blocks — each a strided convolution, a depthwise DConv residual, and a 1×1 rewrite — with the frequency branch compressing along frequency until it collapses to the time axis, while the waveform branch strides in time in parallel. A learned frequency embedding (ScaledEmbedding, L43, injected around line 360 of htdemucs.py) breaks the frequency-axis symmetry, and MultiWrap (MultiWrap, L160) lets outer layers process frequency bands with shared weights.

The Cross-Domain Transformer Bottleneck

At the bottom of both U-Nets — four downsampling stages deep, 48 base channels with a growth factor of two, so 384 channels — the model inserts the transformer. If bottom_channels is set, a pair of 1×1 convolutions first projects both branches to a common width; then crosstransformer runs t_layers = 5 layers per branch. Each layer is a CrossTransformerEncoderLayer (CrossTransformerEncoderLayer, L380) in pre-norm style with a residual LayerScale (LayerScale, L236), and the attention inside is a custom MultiheadAttention (MultiheadAttention, L725) that supports structured sparsity: the mask can be diagonal-band (diag), random, or global-token patterns, mixed freely, which is what keeps 10000-position sequences affordable.

The point of the block is the cross part: after self-attention within each branch, the spectrogram stream queries the waveform stream and vice versa, so low-level timing cues from the waveform can disambiguate spectral overlaps and vice versa. Both updated sequences are returned to the decoder, which mirrors the encoder with skip connections on each side and finally sums the two reconstructed sources in the time domain. It is a clean answer to a classic question in this literature — you rarely have to choose between time-domain and frequency-domain modeling when you can afford both.

From Checkpoint to Stems: The Inference Path

The loader is refreshingly explicit. get_model builds a RemoteRepo from a files.txt index that ships inside the package (REMOTE_ROOT, L21 points into demucs/remote), a BagOnlyRepo that parses the bag YAML files you saw above, and an AnyModelRepo that tries both; there is even a special case that detects a missing diffq dependency from the import error. Once loaded, the model is set to eval and returned.

The engine around the forward pass is where the practical quality lives. apply_model handles three orthogonal tricks. First, bags: it runs each sub-model and averages the estimates with per-source weights. Second, shifts (API default 1): the mixture is randomly shifted by up to half a second, the whole prediction is repeated, and outputs are unshifted and averaged — a cheap test-time ensemble that measurably improves SDR. Third, splitting: the track is cut into model.segment-long chunks with overlap = 0.25, each chunk is predicted independently, and a triangular weighting kernel (built around line 271 of apply.py) cross-fades the joints before a final normalization. On CPU you can pass num_workers and the chunks are submitted to a thread pool. The top-level Separator wraps all of this and handles decoding through AudioFile.read and encoding through save_audio, which supports wav, flac, and mp3 with clip-mode control.

From Install to Your First Model

Install with pip install demucs (or clone the repo and pip install -e .), and make sure ffmpeg is on your PATH — the I/O layer shells out to it for both probing and decoding. Then separate your first track:

demucs -n htdemucs "your_song.mp3"

You will find the four stems under separated/htdemucs/your_song/vocals.wav and friends. Two variations worth trying immediately: htdemucs_ft is the fine-tuned bag of four checkpoints — noticeably better on vocals, roughly four times slower because it averages four full predictions — and --two-stems=vocals writes just the vocal and a karaoke-style complement. The equivalent Python is short:

from demucs.api import Separator

sep = Separator(model="htdemucs")
origin, stems = sep.separate_audio_file("your_song.mp3")
print(stems.keys(), sep.samplerate)

If you use torchaudio (/torchaudio/), note the cross-pollination: torchaudio ships its own HDemucs implementation, and Demucs’s training script can wrap it directly via TorchHDemucsWrapper (TorchHDemucsWrapper, L36) for benchmarking against the same checkpoint metadata. Training your own variant runs through hydra configs: python -m demucs.train builds datasets (Wavset, Wavset, L107, random-crops pre-extracted wav tracks), constructs the optimizer, and hands everything to Solver.train (Solver.train, L172), whose per-epoch loop lives in _run_one_epoch (Solver._run_one_epoch, L291).

Honest Limits

Memory is the first wall. The hybrid model processes ten-second 44.1 kHz stereo segments with two parallel U-Nets plus attention at the bottom, and on consumer GPUs you will hit out-of-memory long before you expect; the segmented apply_model path exists precisely because full-track inference does not fit. CPU-only separation works but is slow — plan minutes per song, not seconds, and use --jobs to parallelize chunks. On Apple silicon the code even detours complex tensors through the CPU because MPS lacks complex support (see the explicit workaround in HTDemucs.forward), so expect the same order of slowness there.

Second, scope: Demucs is a music separator. Speech enhancement, speaker diarization, and transcription belong to other tools entirely — for transcript-oriented audio work, see our tours of /whisperx/ or /pyannote-audio/. Third, quality is checkpoint-dependent: the htdemucs name changed the default model, and the maintainers themselves note it can underperform the older MDX models on some material, which is why bag variants and the --shifts flag exist as tuning knobs rather than conveniences. Finally, training is a serious undertaking — it assumes MUSDB18-HQ, the Dora experiment runner, and multi-GPU patience. For what it is, though, the codebase is a model of restraint: a real production model you can read in an afternoon, and one of the best illustrations that hybrid architectures are not a compromise but a deliberate design.
entry.summary: How facebookresearch/demucs splits a song into stems: the hybrid transformer architecture, the separation driver, audio I/O, and the training loop.

entry.title: DuckDB: An In-Process Analytical SQL Engine, From SQL Text to Row Groups

link.title: DuckDB: An In-Process Analytical SQL Engine, From SQL Text to Row Groups

entry.content:
Most people meet DuckDB as a magic one-liner: pip install duckdb, then SQL that crunches hundreds of millions of rows inside the same Python process that would otherwise have churned through pandas loops. There is no server, no socket, no connection pool to tune. The entire analytical engine — SQL parser, planner, optimizer, execution engine, and storage manager — is linked into your process as a compact C++ library. That design choice is why DuckDB feels more like SQLite than like a warehouse, and it is also why reading its source is unusually rewarding: every stage of a query’s life is a few files away.

The repository is organized almost exactly along that life cycle. src/main owns the client-facing objects (instances, connections, result sets). src/parser turns text into a parse tree, src/planner binds names and types into a logical plan, src/optimizer rewrites that plan with roughly fifty rule passes, and src/execution lowers it to physical operators that src/parallel drives across worker threads. src/storage persists row groups into a single file with MVCC semantics. Each directory maps to a clean interface boundary, which is rare for a codebase of this age and ambition.

One structural note before we dive in: this tour anchors on the main branch as of late October 2026, and the repo layout has shifted underfoot in a way worth knowing. The classic tools/pythonpkg directory — where the duckdb.connect() Python binding lived for years — is no longer in the monorepo; the Python client now evolves in its own dedicated repository. What remains in-core is the C API surface under src/main/capi, which is precisely the layer every client binding, Python included, compiles against. So the “Python surface” in this tour is read from the bottom up: whatever your Python code calls, it lands in the same C++ entry points we will trace below.

The query life cycle across DuckDB's six subsystems: from a connection through parsing, binding, optimization, physical lowering, parallel execution, and row-group storage.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • Everything starts with an instance: DuckDB::DuckDB, L404 constructs a DatabaseInstance whose Initialize, L305 installs settings, loads extensions, and prepares the buffer manager.
  • The same boot sequence calls StartScheduler, L329, spinning up the worker threads that will later execute your query work units.
  • Client code talks to a connection: Connection::Query, L97 is the thin convenience wrapper every binding ultimately funnels into.
  • The real work happens in ClientContext::Query, L904, which takes a lock and delegates to QueryInternal, L935 — the single choke point for statement execution.
  • Text becomes a parse tree in Parser::ParseQuery, L254, which hands statements to the binder.
  • Binder::Bind, L78 dispatches per statement type and produces a bound logical plan; Planner::CreatePlan, L200 owns this handoff.
  • Optimization is a separate, ordered pass list driven by Optimizer::Optimize, L539 before the physical plan generator takes over.
  • On the storage side, DataTable::Scan, L342 serves versioned row-group reads to the scan operators visible at the far right.

From Install to Your First Model

The promise of an in-process engine lands the moment you skip the ETL step. After pip install duckdb, you can query a CSV directly from disk, aggregate a pandas DataFrame in SQL, or hand results to scikit-learn without a single serialization boundary:

import duckdb

con = duckdb.connect()  # in-memory database, no server anywhere
con.execute("CREATE TABLE clicks AS SELECT * FROM read_csv('events/*.csv')")
top = con.sql("""
    SELECT user_id, count(*) AS n, avg(dwell_ms) AS dwell
    FROM clicks WHERE ts > now() - INTERVAL '7' DAY
    GROUP BY user_id ORDER BY n DESC LIMIT 1000
""").arrow()

That .arrow() return type is the quiet superpower for ML work: feature engineering output goes to Apache Arrow, which pandas, Polars, and most modern training stacks consume zero-copy. If your preprocessing currently lives in pandas, DuckDB can replace the hot loops while keeping the same in-memory objects — the pandas interoperability path scans NumPy-backed columns directly, and the sibling Polars engine follows the same columnar philosophy from the Rust side. For teams that build feature stages over a datasets catalog, treating SQL as the feature-definition language is often the cleanest contract between data engineering and model code.

The operational model is also SQLite-like: the database is a single file (or pure memory), connections are cheap, and PRAGMA threads=N or SET memory_limit='4GB' tune resource use per process. Nothing about the surrounding stack needs to change.

The Query Path: Bind, Optimize, Lower

The detail diagram zooms into what happens between the SQL string and the operator tree, and the code is more readable than you might expect.

Inside one query: session preparation, statement binding, the optimizer's rule passes, the physical operator tree, the event-driven scheduler, and the storage layer that feeds it.

Binding is where SQL gets real. Binder::Bind(SelectStatement &), L8 resolves each table reference into a LogicalGet, each expression into a typed tree, and each join into a logical operator with explicit column bindings. Errors you know from practice — “column X does not exist”, ambiguous references, type mismatches — are thrown here, before any optimization.

The optimizer phase is a sequence of named passes, each a small, testable rewrite. Two representative ones: FilterPushdown::Rewrite, L108 walks the tree pushing predicates toward the data sources so scans can skip row groups entirely, while StatisticsPropagator::PropagateStatistics, L66 pushes cardinality and min/max information upward so join order and aggregation strategy can be chosen with evidence rather than guesses. Because the passes run in a fixed order inside RunBuiltInOptimizers, L186, the system behaves deterministically — and EXPLAIN output maps back onto these rewrites one-to-one.

Lowering is the recursive walk driven by PhysicalPlanGenerator::CreatePlan, L75. Every logical operator gets a physical counterpart: a LogicalGet becomes a scan that emits DataChunks, a hash join becomes a build/probe pair with a shared hash table, and aggregation becomes a radix-partitioned machine that can absorb unbounded key cardinality. The generator also wires the sink/source contract that the scheduler depends on: every operator exposes either a source, a sink, or both, plus state objects created once globally and once per thread.

Prepared statements follow a shorter path on repeat runs: ClientContext::Prepare, L671 binds once and caches the plan, so the second and thousandth executions skip parsing and binding entirely. Embedded clients that want a stable ABI without C++ linkage go through the versioned C API instead — duckdb_v2_connection_create, L5 hands out a handle whose functions mirror the C++ connection almost one-to-one.

Inside the Execution Engine

DuckDB’s execution story is morsel-driven parallelism. Rather than partitioning by operator, the engine decomposes query execution into dependency-ordered work units, and worker threads cooperate on shared operator state. Executor::ScheduleEventsInternal, L83 builds that event graph: scans first, then build sides, then probes and sinks, with events rescheduling successors as they complete. Tasks are dispatched to TaskScheduler::ScheduleTask, L64, whose queues feed the worker pool started at instance boot.

Three data-structure choices make this fast. First, chunks are vectors of roughly 2048 values, so per-row virtual-call overhead is amortized: ExpressionExecutor::Execute, L86 evaluates expression trees over whole vectors, dispatching once per operation rather than once per row. Second, operator state is split into global and local halves — GetGlobalSourceState, L132 and GetLocalSourceState, L127 — so threads touch shared structures rarely and their own state constantly. Third, when work must cross threads (a hash table’s build side feeding many probes, an aggregate’s partitions being combined), it flows through a ColumnDataCollection, the chunked columnar buffer defined in src/common/types/column, which can spill to disk under memory pressure rather than fail.

The hash operators show the payoff concretely. PhysicalHashJoin::Sink, L899 has every thread append its build-side chunk in parallel before a single finalize event flips the table to probe mode, and PhysicalHashAggregate::Sink, L434 does the same for grouped aggregation with radix partitioning to bound contention. Neither operator knows how it was scheduled; the event graph decides, and the same code runs single-threaded on a laptop and wide on a 64-core machine.

Storage: Row Groups, Blocks, Checkpoints

Persistence follows the same chunk-first philosophy. Tables are sequences of row groups (large blocks of rows compressed column-wise), and DataTable::Append, L1116 adds new chunks under transactional versioning: writers allocate row versions, readers filter by snapshot, and neither blocks the other in the common case. Scans like the one feeding PhysicalTableScan::GetDataInternal, L162 iterate row groups, apply zone-map filters from metadata, and decompress only what survives.

Ingest-side table functions are the other half of the story. ReadCSVTableFunction::GetFunction, L195 registers the parallel CSV reader whose sniffer infers types, and the multi-file machinery in MultiFileReader::Create, L40 globs directories, unifies schemas, and lets one read_csv or read_parquet call range over thousands of files. Hive-style partition pruning rides on the same reader, which is why partitioned Parquet trees filter almost for free.

The on-disk format is a single file managed by the block manager: SingleFileBlockManager::WriteHeader, L1333 commits metadata updates by writing a new header with a checksummed version, so crashes leave the previous consistent state intact. Checkpointing is explicit and compaction-oriented — SingleFileCheckpointWriter::CreateCheckpoint, L235 rewrites row groups in place and clears the write-ahead log — and CHECKPOINT can be invoked manually after bulk loads to keep scans dense.

Honest Limits

The in-process design that makes DuckDB pleasant also defines its edges. One process, one writer: multiple processes cannot safely open the same database file for writes, so the “just point two services at it” deployment does not exist; if you need concurrent writers across machines, you are looking at a different class of system. RAM discipline matters too — memory_limit is a real ceiling, and while most operators spill gracefully, adversarial workloads (very high-cardinality grouped aggregates, skewed joins) can still push latency rather than throughput into the failure mode.

For the Python user there is a governance reality worth tracking: the binding lives in its own repository now, which means version skew between the core engine and the client package is possible in a way it was not when both shipped from one tree. The vectorized engine also has a learning curve at its edges — deep customization (new operator types, custom file formats) requires C++ and a rebuild, not a plugin script. And while the optimizer is excellent, it is rule-and-statistics based, not learned: pathological cardinality estimates on uncorrelated predicates remain possible, and EXPLAIN ANALYZE is still the honest arbiter.

None of these are disqualifying for the engine’s sweet spot — local analytics, feature engineering, embedded dashboards, file-format shoveling — and that sweet spot covers a surprising share of what data teams actually do. What the source tour adds is the ability to predict behavior: knowing that filters push down to row groups tells you how to order your columns; knowing that hash builds flip at a finalize event tells you why some joins stream and others materialize. The code rewards exactly this kind of reading.
entry.summary: A source tour of DuckDB's C++ core: how a SQL string becomes a bound plan, an optimized physical operator tree, and parallel columnar scans over row groups.

entry.title: Numba, From @jit to Machine Code: A Source Tour of the LLVM-Based JIT Compiler for Python

link.title: Numba, From @jit to Machine Code: A Source Tour of the LLVM-Based JIT Compiler for Python

entry.content:
Numba occupies a unique spot in the Python performance world: it is a compiler that ships as a pip package. You put a decorator on a plain Python function, call the function once, and by the time that call returns, your Python bytecode has been type-inferred, translated into LLVM IR, optimized, and emitted as machine code for your exact CPU. Every later call skips Python entirely and jumps straight into the native function pointer. There is no separate build step, no C toolchain to drive, and no Ahead-of-Time ceremony — the compiler is embedded in the library and runs lazily, at import time of the call, not of the module.

In this source tour we read the numba/numba repository the way its authors layered it. The story runs through five territories: the decorator entry points (numba/core/decorators.py, numba/core/dispatcher.py), the interpreter that lifts bytecode into Numba’s own IR (numba/core/interpreter.py), the type inference engine (numba/core/typing/, numba/core/typeinfer.py), the lowering and code generation layers (numba/core/lowering.py, numba/core/codegen.py), and the accelerators — numba/parfors/ for automatic CPU parallelism and numba/cuda/ for NVIDIA GPUs. Along the way we will point at exact classes and line numbers so you can follow the same path in the code.

Why care about a numeric JIT on an AI blog? Because the techniques here are the same ones underneath every serious ML runtime: PyTorch’s compilation stack, tinygrad’s kernel generation, and the C metaprogramming in llm.c all solve the problem “turn high-level array math into tight machine code” in related ways. Numba is the cleanest open-source classroom for that subject because each stage is a separate, readable Python module.

The overview: a call enters through the decorators and the Dispatcher, becomes Numba IR, gets typed by the constraint engine, is rewritten for auto-parallelism, then lowered to LLVM and machine code — with the CUDA target reusing the same skeleton.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • @jit, L27 — the single public entry point; it accepts a function or a signature and composes target, locals, and options into a dispatcher factory.
  • @njit, L250 — a thin alias that pins nopython=True, the mode you should always use; the old object-mode fallback is gone from modern versions.
  • Dispatcher, L757 — the callable object your decorated name actually refers to; it keeps one compiled specialization per argument-type signature.
  • Interpreter, L1423 — walks CPython bytecode and rebuilds it as Numba IR, a typed-node SSA-friendly representation.
  • TypeInferer, L952 — the constraint solver that decides every variable’s Numba type before any code is generated.
  • Lower, L346 — walks the typed IR one instruction at a time and emits equivalent LLVM IR through llvmlite.
  • JITCPUCodegen, L1364 — hands the LLVM modules to the optimization and back-end layers and produces executable machine code.
  • ParforPass, L2975 — the auto-parallelizer that recognizes loop and NumPy patterns and rewrites them into Parfor nodes.
  • CUDACompiler, L119 — proof that the whole skeleton is target-agnostic: the GPU path subclasses the same base and swaps in an NVVM back end.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is deliberately boring: pip install numba pulls in llvmlite (the LLVM binding layer) plus a small set of dependencies — no compilers to install, no CUDA toolkit required unless you want the GPU path. The classic first model is a numerical kernel; here is a logistic-regression-style update, which is exactly the shape of code Numba loves:

import numpy as np
from numba import njit

@njit(cache=True, fastmath=True)
def train_step(w, X, y, lr):
    n = X.shape[0]
    for i in range(n):
        pred = 1.0 / (1.0 + np.exp(-(X[i] @ w)))
        err = y[i] - pred
        w += lr * err * X[i]
    return w

The first call is where everything interesting happens. train_step(X, y, ...) is not a Python function anymore — it is a CPUDispatcher, L44. Its call path enters _compile_for_args, L342, which maps each Python argument to a Numba type using machinery like resolve_value_type, L441. A float64 NumPy array becomes array(float64, 1d, C); that tuple of types is the cache key. If a compiled specialization for this key already exists — on disk too, thanks to cache=True — the call is a pointer jump. If not, the dispatcher blocks and runs the whole compile stack described below, then stores the result. This is why the first call can take hundreds of milliseconds while every subsequent call runs 30–100x faster than CPython. In a serving loop you warm the kernel once and pay native prices forever after; the same lazy-compile discipline shows up in other runtimes we have covered, from PyTorch’s compilation features to tinygrad’s JIT.

The Stage List: How a Compile Actually Proceeds

Every compilation is a sequence of small passes threaded through one mutable state object. compile_extra, L713 is the target-facing entry: it builds a CompilerBase, L386 subclass — Compiler for the CPU — whose state carries the function, the flags, the typing context, and later the IR and the LLVM module. DefaultPassBuilder, L528 assembles the nopython compilation stages by concatenating three lists: the untyped passes, the typed passes, and the lowering passes.

The executor is deliberately simple. PassManager, L169 holds an ordered list of stage descriptors, and its run, L342 method walks that list, fetching each registered stage from the PassRegistry, L408 and executing it. Stages subclass CompilerPass, L31; most are FunctionPass, L116 instances that mutate the IR in place. That is the entire control flow — there is no scheduler, no planner, just an ordered list you can print with NUMBA_DEBUG_ARRAY_OPT or the -O debug flags.

The untyped half of the sequence lives in numba/core/untyped_passes.py. TranslateByteCode, L73 invokes the interpreter to build func_ir; IRProcessing, L112 performs post-processing on the freshly built IR; and ReconstructSSA, L1745 rewrites the IR into static single assignment form, which is what makes the later rewrites and the type solver well-behaved. In between sit dozens of small rewrites — closure inlining, literal unrolling, dead branch pruning — each one an independent, testable class.

The Detail View: Inside Each Stage

The detail diagram spreads the same story across all six territories, including the stage machinery and the two accelerators, with the exact files each participant lives in.

The detail view: the Dispatcher-to-compile_extra handshake on the left, the untyped and typed stage lists in the middle, the LLVM code generation layers on the right, and the parfors plus CUDA accelerators along the bottom.

Type Inference: The Constraint Engine

Typing is where Numba earns its speed. The frontend builds a TypeInferer over the SSA IR; build_constraint, L1033 inspects each IR instruction and registers constraints — assignments propagate types between variables, calls register a CallConstraint, and so on. Then propagate, L1064 iterates the constraint network until it reaches a fixpoint: every variable must end up with exactly one Numba type, and inference failures raise the famous long TypingError diagnostics rather than falling back to slow code.

Resolving what a call means is delegated to the typing context. BaseContext, L210 is the registry of everything the compiler knows how to type, and resolve_function_type, L268 is the hot entry every CallConstraint eventually hits. It consults typing templates: AbstractTemplate, L349 subclasses implement a generic() method that, given argument types, returns a candidate Signature, L27 — return type plus argument types. NumPy functions, math functions, array indexing, @overload implementations: all of them register templates into this context. When inference succeeds, the IR is annotated and ready for lowering; when it fails, the error message lists every candidate signature that was tried, which is the single most useful debugging surface in the whole project.

Lowering to LLVM and Machine Code

The typed stage list ends with the lowering passes. NativeLowering, L517 constructs the lowering driver — BaseLower, L25 sets up the LLVM function declaration, the code library, and the variable-to-LLVM-value map — and then Lower, L346 runs the main lower, L188 loop over the IR. Each instruction is handed to lower_inst, L457, which dispatches on the node kind: an assignment lowers through the operation implementations registered in numba/core/imputils.py, a control-flow node lowers to LLVM branches, a Parfor node gets its own dedicated lowering path in numba/parfors/parfor_lowering.py.

The final stage is NoPythonBackend, L569: it asks the target context to optimize the finished LLVM module and produce the callable. On the CPU path that work happens in numba/core/codegen.py, where the Codegen, L1130 base defines the contract and JITCodeLibrary, L984 accumulates modules until JITCPUCodegen, L1364 runs the LLVM optimization passes and the native back end, then hands back a raw function pointer wrapped into the dispatcher. Environment arrays, exception state, and the boxing/unboxing glue between Python objects and native values are all woven in at this layer. It is code generation in the same family as tinygrad’s kernel emitter or llm.c’s hand-rolled GGML loops — just with LLVM doing the instruction selection.

Auto-Parallelism and the GPU Path

Pass parallel=True to @njit and the typed stage list grows a pair of extra stages. PreParforPass, L1514 rewrites convenient syntax — prange loops, in-place operators, reductions — into canonical forms, then ParforPass, L2975 pattern-matches loops and NumPy expressions and replaces them with a Parfor, L633 IR node: an explicit, analyzable parallel loop carrying its own loop nests, array analysis, and scheduling information. Array analysis proves bounds and independence so fusion and privatization are legal. At lowering time the choice in DefaultPassBuilder between NativeParforLowering, L528 and the scalar path decides whether those nodes become OpenMP-parallel loops. The same subsystem powers @vectorize, L64 and guvectorize, L139, which broadcast a scalar kernel across arrays exactly like NumPy ufuncs — a natural companion to the NumPy compatibility story.

The GPU path reuses the whole skeleton with different concrete classes. @cuda.jit, L14 decorates a device kernel; the resulting CUDADispatcher, L580 compiles the kernel through CUDACompiler, L119, whose typed back end is CUDABackend, L68, and emits PTX via JITCUDACodegen, L351 driving NVVM instead of the CPU back end. Thread indexing (threadIdx, shared memory, barriers) is expressed inside the kernel body, so the frontend and typing layers barely change — a nice demonstration that the decorator-to-LLVM design generalizes.

Honest Limits

The first-call compile latency is real and unavoidable: warm every specialization before serving traffic, or the cache file pays for it. The nopython subset excludes large parts of dynamic Python — arbitrary class hierarchies, mixed-type dicts, most reflection — and the failure mode is a TypingError whose wall of text you must learn to read from the bottom up. parallel=True needs a working threading layer (OpenMP or TBB) and its speedups depend on array analysis succeeding; when the analyzer cannot prove independence it silently stays serial. The CUDA target requires an NVIDIA GPU, the CUDA toolkit, and driver versions in a supported window, and it compiles for your specific compute capability. Caching interacts poorly with closures and with functions defined in notebooks, where the source-to-cache-key mapping changes between sessions. And while numba composes beautifully with NumPy, it is not a general ML graph compiler: no autodiff, no dynamic shapes, no kernel-fusion planners at the scale of the deep-learning runtimes. Its sweet spot is exactly one thing — making a numerical Python function run at native speed — and within that scope it remains one of the best-engineered compilers you can read.
entry.summary: How numba turns a decorated Python function into LLVM IR and native machine code: dispatch, type inference, lowering, parfor parallelism, and CUDA.

entry.title: OpenCV Source Tour: From the Mat Container to the DNN Engine Inside the World’s Default Vision Library

link.title: OpenCV Source Tour: From the Mat Container to the DNN Engine Inside the World’s Default Vision Library

entry.content:
OpenCV is the library that every other computer vision tool gets compared to. Twenty-plus years in, it is the default import in tutorials, the runtime under countless factory robots and security cameras, and the compatibility target that newer frameworks measure themselves against — Kornia, for instance, exists precisely because OpenCV’s kernels are not differentiable, and MediaPipe leans on the same C++ sensibility for its own graph machinery. Yet despite the ubiquity, surprisingly few people have read the source. The repository looks monolithic, the C++ is dense, and the Python experience is so smooth that the machinery underneath becomes invisible. This post is a tour of that machinery on the 5.x branch, which is now the default branch of opencv/opencv.

The repository is organized as a set of self-contained modules under modules/, and each module is effectively a layered library: a public header API on top, dispatch code that selects CPU SIMD paths or GPU paths in the middle, and algorithmic kernels at the bottom. We narrowed the tour to the four modules that matter most for the cv2 experience: core (the Mat container, the allocator, the thread pool, the OpenCL runtime, and the FileStorage serializer), imgproc (the classic kernels: resize, blur, edges, color conversions), dnn (the inference engine that reads ONNX and other formats), and python (the binding generator and runtime bridge that turns all of the above into a single importable module).

The method is the same as in our other source tours: we mapped the subsystems into two architecture diagrams — an overview and a detail view — and then walked each one with line-linked references, so every claim below links to a real function at a real line that you can open in your browser. A note on scope: this is a genuinely large codebase (the four modules we checked out contain over seven thousand files), so the tour favors the load-bearing files over exhaustive coverage.

The overview graph: a Python call enters through the binding bridge, lands in a reference-counted Mat, flows through imgproc kernels or the DNN engine, and threads and OpenCL contexts fan the work out underneath.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The bridge. PyInit_cv2, L621 is the CPython module entry point; it delegates to init_body, L482, which registers every generated submodule, type, and constant you see under import cv2. The special method pycvRegisterMatType, L105 lets the NumPy-facing wrapper register its own Mat type back into the module.
  • Conversion. pyopencv_to, L75 is the workhorse that turns a Python object into a cv::Mat, typically by borrowing a NumPy buffer rather than copying it. Around it live two RAII helpers in cv2_util.hpp, L22 and L34: PyAllowThreads drops the GIL so C++ workers can run concurrently, and PyEnsureGIL reacquires it when callbacks need Python again.
  • The container. Everything pixel-shaped is a Mat. Mat::create, L1072 allocates or reshapes it, backed by the cache-line-aligned allocator fastMalloc, L130. The GPU shadow twin is UMat::create, L360, whose buffers live in an OpenCL context built by initializeContextFromHandle, L3220.
  • Persistence. FileStorage::open, L2028 parses and writes YAML, XML, and JSON documents, and FileStorage::operator[], L2111 returns a FileNode cursor for key lookups. This is the machinery under cv::imwrite, camera calibration files, and model configuration files.
  • Kernels. cv::resize, L3580 dispatches to interpolation-specific implementations; the generic path builds a per-row resizeGeneric_Invoker, L1785 and hands it to the thread pool. GaussianBlur, L526 runs separable row and column filters in parallel, and Canny, L683 computes gradients and then tracks edges with its own parallelCanny, L220 loop body.
  • Color. cvtColor, L192 is one giant conversion switch covering dozens of color space pairs, each with an OpenCL fast path attempted first.
  • Inference. readNet, L13 auto-detects the model format and lands ONNX files at readNetFromONNX, L72. At run time, Net::forward, L76 delegates into the implementation, which validates the backend, fuses layers, and executes them one by one.

The Detail View: Following One Call Through the Stack

The detail graph expands each group: the binding internals on the left, the core runtime that everything shares, the imgproc kernels, and the DNN frontend feeding the layer zoo and backend dispatch.

Follow net.forward() from Python and the detail graph comes alive. The public Net::forward, L76 is three lines of assertion plus a delegate. The implementation first runs Net::Impl::setUpNet, L190, which validates the backend and target pair and allocates every layer’s blobs. If this is the first forward pass, graph optimization kicks in: Net::Impl::fuseLayers, L35 merges convolution + batch norm + scale + activation chains into single nodes, which is where most of the real-world speedup of OpenCV’s inference lives. Then execution proceeds layer by layer through Net::Impl::forwardLayer, L698, which looks up the layer’s backend node via the preferableBackend, L143 dispatch, falls back to the CPU implementation when no specialized backend claims the layer, and optionally runs the whole thing on OpenCL UMat blobs.

The layer zoo is where the 5.x branch gets interesting. The classic float path still lives in ConvolutionLayerImpl, L200, but a new engine has appeared alongside it: Conv2LayerImpl, L34 with explicit parallel tile loops, GemmLayerImpl, L55 with threaded GEMM blocks, and — the headline — SDPALayerImpl, L15, scaled dot-product attention. Combined with KVCacheManager::reserve, L143, which wires per-layer key-value caches into the net, OpenCV’s DNN module is quietly becoming capable of running autoregressive transformer models, not just convolutional classifiers.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is one pip command, and the first useful program exercises both halves of the graph — classic kernels and the inference engine:

import cv2
import numpy as np

# classic imgproc path: color, blur, edges
img = cv2.imread("scene.jpg")
gray = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)   # color.cpp dispatch
gray = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)       # smooth.dispatch.cpp
edges = cv2.Canny(gray, 50, 150)               # canny.cpp

# dnn path: ONNX model inference
net = cv2.dnn.readNetFromONNX("mobilenetv2.onnx")
blob = cv2.dnn.blobFromImage(img, scalefactor=1.0/255.0,
                             size=(224, 224), swapRB=True)
net.setInput(blob)
out = net.forward()                            # net.cpp -> net_impl.cpp
print(out.shape)                               # (1, 1000, ...)

A few practical notes that the source makes obvious. First, cv2.GaussianBlur and cv2.Canny release the GIL while they run (every generated binding wraps its call in PyAllowThreads), which means you can run multiple OpenCV calls from multiple Python threads and actually get parallelism — a rare property among Python libraries. Second, the blob preprocessing in cv2.dnn.blobFromImage exists because the DNN module expects normalized, channel-swapped, batched float tensors; the conversion from your BGR uint8 Mat to that layout is explicit rather than magical. Third, if the model output looks wrong, check the channel order first: the library’s BGR convention leaks everywhere, which is exactly the friction Kornia was built to eliminate for PyTorch users. For detection and segmentation models that consume these edge and blob outputs, our Ultralytics and ONNX tours cover the consumer side.

Under the Hood: Threads, Memory, and the GIL

Three systems make every kernel above fast, and they are worth reading in their own right. The thread pool entry point parallel_for_, L513 takes a Range and a loop body, and its implementation parallel_for_impl, L558 decides whether to use the internal pool, TBB, or OpenMP, splitting the range into stripes sized by the caller’s hint. setNumThreads, L722 caps the worker count globally, and it is the first knob to reach for when OpenCV oversubscribes a container that already runs its own pool. Memory management is deliberately boring: fastMalloc, L130 allocates aligned blocks, and Mat reference counting means the Python side can pass buffers around without deep copies as long as nobody writes in place — the reason Canny refuses in-place input for RGB sources (see the assertion at Canny, L683). And when a kernel claims GPU capability, it is usually the UMat path through the OpenCL runtime in ocl.cpp, whose contexts and command queues are constructed independently of any particular framework — a design that keeps OpenCV usable on machines where CUDA is not an option.

What the 5.x Branch Changes

The default branch is no longer the 4.x you may have pinned. Three shifts stand out from the source. The DNN module is growing transformer-native layers — attention, GEMM, rotary embeddings, RMSNorm, and the KV cache manager — moving it from “runs MobileNet” toward “runs small language models,” which changes what cv2.dnn is for. The binding generator under modules/python/src2 now also produces typing stubs (typing_stubs_generator.py), so IDE autocompletion for cv2 comes from the same headers that generate the C++ wrappers, keeping signatures honest. And the codebase continues its long migration toward pluggable engine selection inside DNN: the ONNX reader resolves between the built-in engine and ONNX Runtime when built with WITH_ONNXRUNTIME, an early example of what is effectively a modular inference strategy inside the library.

Honest Limits

The C++ weight is real. The Python layer is generated glue; when something misbehaves you end up reading C++ stacks, and the binding generator’s conventions (in-place output arrays, None handling, NumPy striding) are a language of their own. The DNN module is inference-only — there is no training story here, so it complements rather than replaces the training frameworks we have covered. Performance is uneven across the matrix of backends and targets: the CPU SIMD paths are excellent and battle-tested, but the CUDA, Vulkan, and WebNN backends each cover different op subsets, and a model that runs on one target may silently fall back to CPU per-layer on another, which is why net_impl.cpp carries explicit backend-unsupported errors. The UMat/OpenCL path is portable but its speed depends heavily on your vendor’s OpenCL runtime. Finally, 5.x is a moving default branch: the line numbers linked here are accurate today, and the transformer-era DNN layers in particular are still visibly under construction.

If you want the differentiable counterpart to everything in imgproc, read Kornia next; if you want to see where these pixels go in production systems, MediaPipe shows the graph-execution descendant of the same design school.
entry.summary: A guided source tour of opencv/opencv on the 5.x branch: the Mat array container, parallel image kernels, the cv2 Python bridge, and a DNN module growing transformer layers.
